items.description: The Ledger’s account of Syd and Diane Mandelbaum’s food-recovery work and the contractual mechanism that helped turn surplus into community support.

items.headline: Film Biz Recycling
items.caption: Eva Radke · The Lightning Point
items.description: Explore Eva Radke’s Film Biz Recycling, the creative-reuse warehouse and community connections built from what productions leave behind. Based on a conversation in July 2026.

items.headline: EcoSet
items.caption: The Proof of Durability
items.description: The Ledger follows EcoSet’s embedded sustainability crews and materials reuse, from a Minneapolis prototype to a lasting Los Angeles operation.

items.headline: Earth Angel
items.caption: The East Coast Pioneer
items.description: Explore Emellie O’Brien’s Earth Angel, its work on production sustainability, and the next chapter after its merger with TheGreenShot.

items.headline: Skater Girl
items.caption: A skatepark built before the film
items.description: Vinati and Manjari Makijany built a permanent skatepark for a Rajasthan community before making the film. Explore the Ledger’s account, informed by a conversation with Vinati in August 2026.

items.headline: Sing Sing
items.caption: The Equity Model
items.description: Explore the Ledger’s account of Sing Sing and an approach to shared ownership and equal pay that asks who participates in a film’s value.

items.headline: Motion Picture Relief Fund
items.caption: A century of care for film workers
items.description: From Mary Pickford’s collection pail to a lasting institution of care, the Ledger traces mutual aid within the film community.

items.headline: The Lord of the Rings
items.caption: Hobbiton · The set that stayed
items.description: A film set became a lasting destination. The Ledger explores Hobbiton’s benefits and the distinctions between tourism, sustainability and community giving.

items.headline: Field of Dreams
items.caption: The Accidental Asset
items.description: A baseball diamond built for a film remained open after the production left. The Ledger follows the gift, the stewardship and the complications that followed.

items.headline: Wicked
items.caption: The Ecological Choice
items.description: Explore the Ledger’s account of the film’s tulip fields, their afterlife as a charity attraction, and what this example does and does not show.

items.headline: Interstellar
items.caption: What if the harvest had become a gift?
items.description: The Ledger asks what else a film’s real cornfield might have made possible. A missed-opportunity case, not a claim that its harvest was donated.

items.headline: Patch Adams
items.caption: The gift and the unfulfilled hope
items.description: The film supported work at the Gesundheit Institute. The Ledger also examines the hospital hope that went unfulfilled and the difference between a gift and a promise.

items.headline: Black Panther
items.caption: Wakanda in the Real World
items.description: Explore the giving around Black Panther, including support for STEM education and communities, alongside the Ledger’s questions about scale and opportunity.

items.headline: Slumdog Millionaire
items.caption: The Trust That Could Only Do So Much
items.description: The Ledger examines charitable giving and the trust created for two child actors, including what that support could and could not resolve.

items.headline: Braddock Free Store
items.caption: The Proof of Demand
items.description: Explore how production surplus reached Braddock’s Free Store through community relationships, and what this reveals about the need for a repeatable connection.

items.headline: Balan’s bus stop stays with the community
items.caption: Kerala, India · A film set in daily use
items.description: Residents asked the crew to leave a bus stop built for Balan: The Boy. Reporting describes its continued use by the community after filming.

items.headline: The Last of Us funds a youth legacy project
items.caption: High River, Alberta · A reported contribution
items.description: Reporting describes a $100,000 contribution for a bike park, pump track and playground. The Ledger flags the need to confirm what was built and is open.

items.context: Social Effects NJ · Essays by Bret Warshawsky
items.headline: The stories behind the possibilities
items.caption: Filmanthropy, people and the future of filmmaking.
items.description: Read longer essays by Bret Warshawsky on the people, histories and ideas expanding what filmmaking can give, including Women Are the Story.

items.headline: What Their Work Makes Possible
items.caption: Women Are the Story
items.description: The film itself is already a gift. This essay follows women who helped filmmaking give in further ways: Mary Pickford helped organize care for film workers; Eva Radke connected production surplus with people who could use it; Vinati and Manjari Makijany helped create a skatepark that remained after filming.
items.metadataTitle: What Their Work Makes Possible: Women Are the Story | Social Effects NJ
items.articleImageAlt: Mary Pickford, cover portrait for Women Are the Story

items.headline: Filmmaking as a Human and Civic Act
items.caption: Why Filmmaking’s Future Is Human and Civic
items.description: A film’s value includes the human undertaking that brings it into being: people learning a craft, earning a living, working together and contributing to a place. This original note asks how those gifts might shape filmmaking’s future as AI changes the images we can create.
items.metadataTitle: Filmmaking as a Human and Civic Act: Why Filmmaking’s Future Is Human and Civic | Social Effects NJ
items.articleImageAlt: A film projector casting a golden heart

items.headline: A Century of Giving Through Film
items.caption: The Giants Who Did It First
items.description: Giving through film has a history that long predates today’s language of social impact. This essay traces people and precedents from that history, showing how filmmakers have extended their work’s gifts beyond the screen and offering starting points for what productions could make possible next.
items.metadataTitle: A Century of Giving Through Film: The Giants Who Did It First | Social Effects NJ
items.articleImageAlt: Historic World Film Producing Studios backlot in Fort Lee, New Jersey

items.headline: What We Become Through Making
items.caption: The Irreplaceable Art of Being Human
items.description: Making art changes the people who make it. This essay explores the experience of creating together: rehearsal, vulnerability, trust, discovery and the relationships formed around a shared undertaking. As AI expands what we can generate, Bret asks how the value of those experiences might become more visible, and how the tools could help people collaborate without making the finished output our only measure of the work.
items.metadataTitle: The Irreplaceable Art of Being Human | Social Effects NJ · Deeper Dives
items.articleImageAlt: The Irreplaceable Art of Being Human, AI and Filmmaking: the original orange and gold article cover

items.headline: A Larger Purpose for Making Films
items.caption: When AI Can Make the Movie, Why Make One Together?
items.description: If AI can create compelling films, why gather people to make one together? The experience itself has value: shared attention, learning, trust and changes in the people taking part, even when a film is not a hit.
items.metadataTitle: When AI Can Make the Movie, Why Make One Together? | Social Effects NJ · Deeper Dives
